tagline: Grocery list that stays in sync between everyone in the house.
verdictSummary: A shared list looks trivial and is not, because the requirement is not "a list" — it is two phones in a supermarket, one with no signal, both crossing items off, and neither of them losing an item. That is real-time sync with offline conflict handling, which CONTRIBUTING names as a `kinda` gap for good reason. The rest of AnyList — recipes, meal plans, categorised aisles — genuinely is a weekend.
coreLoopDIY: Keep one shared list per household, add items from recipes, sort them by aisle, and cross them off from any phone in the shop.
whatYouLose: sync that survives two people editing offline at once
the iOS and Android apps, plus Watch and Siri support
the item catalogue that already knows which aisle mustard belongs in
sharing that works when the other person is not technical
recipe web import maintained against sites that keep changing
whyPeopleStillPay: Ten dollars a year, and the other people in your house will actually use it — which is the only requirement a shared shopping list has.
prompt:
Build a shared household shopping list as an offline-first web app, and treat the sync as the feature rather than the plumbing.

The data model is a list of items, each with a name, a quantity, a category and a checked flag. What makes it work is how updates merge. Give every item a stable id generated on the client and store per-field last-write-wins timestamps; represent a deletion as a tombstone with a timestamp rather than a removed row. Two people crossing off different items offline must merge cleanly, and the same item crossed off twice must stay crossed off rather than flapping.

Write that as a test before writing the UI: two clients, both offline, one adds and checks items while the other deletes and re-adds, then both reconnect. Assert the final state on both. This is the whole engineering content of the project.

Categories come from a local mapping file — item name to aisle — that you extend as you shop, so the list sorts into supermarket order. Ship it with a starter mapping of a few hundred common items and let unknown items land in "other" rather than guessing.

Add recipes: a recipe is a name and a list of ingredients with quantities; adding a recipe to the list merges its ingredients, summing quantities where units match and listing them separately where they do not.

Run it as a progressive web app with a service worker so it opens and works in a shop basement, and put it behind a shared login simple enough that someone who does not care about any of this can use it.

Do not build a barcode-scanning pantry inventory in the same project. Tracking what you already have is a different discipline with a much higher abandonment rate, and bolting it on is how a working list app becomes an unused one.

faq.q: Can I import my AnyList data?
faq.a: Partly. AnyList exports recipes in a structured format that maps cleanly onto a recipe table. Lists themselves are transient and not worth migrating — you will have a new one by Thursday.

faq.q: Will the rest of my household actually use it?
faq.a: That is the real question, and the honest answer is that a self-hosted URL behind a login is a harder sell than an app store install. Build for the phone browser, add it to their home screen for them, and expect one conversation about why the app icon is a bookmark.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: A few dollars a month for a small always-on host, which is more than the ten dollars a year AnyList charges. This one is not a money-saving rebuild; it is an ownership one.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Being trusted by everyone in the house. AnyList works the first time on every phone, and a shared list that one person refuses to open is not a shared list.
